reason: The quote states the Failover Testing feature tests resiliency by disabling the BGP session and can be used from the console or the API.
Under the failover test heading the quote gives a configurable duration of minimum 1 minute and maximum 180 minutes and says the test can be cancelled while running.
The quote states test history is preserved for 365 days and is deleted when the virtual interface is deleted.
Under the heading on who can initiate a failover test, the quote says only the owner of the account that includes the virtual interface can initiate it.
The quote states failure detection can be improved with DPD for VPN links and BFD for Direct Connect links.

The quote supports up to 100 routes per BGP session, but the qualifier condition about prefix controls up to 1,000 and 'not examinable yet' is not in the quote (it comes from another page), and adjustable=false is not stated by the quote.
The quote states Direct Connect bypasses the internet and uses dedicated, private network connections between your network and AWS.

The quote supports needing a public VIF and importing all Anycast routes when filtering, but the claim's scope (CloudFront with an origin in your own data center) stands only in the FAQ heading and the preceding sentence, not in the quote; the quote alone never mentions CloudFront.
The quote defines a dedicated connection as a 1/10/100/400 Gbps port dedicated to a single customer and hosted connections as sourced from a Direct Connect Partner.
The quote states a Direct Connect gateway gives access to any Region from any Direct Connect location, excluding China.
The quote states the AWS side ASN cannot be modified after creation and the gateway can be deleted and recreated with the desired private ASN.
The quote defines the gateway as a grouping of VGWs and private VIFs, globally available, created in any Region and accessed from all others.
The quote states an unattached VGW cannot be associated with a Direct Connect gateway.
The quote states no CloudHub support and that a Site-to-Site VPN to a VGW associated with the gateway can be used for failover.
The quote says the gateway only routes from VIFs to VGWs associated with VPCs and that VPC-to-VPC traffic needs a VPC peering connection.

The quote supports sharing a private VIF with up to 20 VPCs to reduce BGP sessions, but the material scope 'with a Direct Connect gateway' stands only in the list lead-in and heading, not in the quote; alone the quote reads as a property of any private VIF.
The quote states traffic takes the shortest path to the destination Region regardless of the location's home Region.
The quote states a gateway with a transit VIF cannot also host a private VIF and is dedicated to the transit VIF.
The quote states up to six transit gateways per Direct Connect gateway as long as announced CIDR blocks do not overlap.
The quote recommends connections at multiple Direct Connect locations for high availability.
Under the LAG mode heading the quote says they are active/active and AWS ports send LACPDUs continuously.
The quote defines a LAG as a logical interface using LACP to aggregate dedicated connections at one endpoint, treated as one connection, with configuration applied to all.
The quote states a maximum of 4 links for 1 or 10 Gbps and 2 links for 100 or 400 Gbps connections.
Under the minimum links ordering heading the quote says minimum links defaults to zero when not selected.
The quote defines minimum links and gives the four ports, minimum three, two active example.
Under the heading asking about mixing 1/10/100/400 Gbps ports, the quote answers no and says a LAG uses the same type of ports.
Under the local preference failover heading the quote describes advertising over the primary VIF with a higher local preference community than the backup.
The quote states a Site-to-Site VPN cannot back up a Direct Connect connection to a Local Zone and two or more Direct Connect connections are needed for redundancy.
The quote states you need a MACsec-capable device on your end of the connection to a Direct Connect location.
The quote defines MACsec as an IEEE standard for confidentiality, integrity and origin authenticity, encrypting from your network or collocated device to the chosen point of presence.
The quote gives 3 notifications at 14, 7 and 1 calendar days and emergency maintenance at any time with up to 60-minute notification depending on its nature (kept in the qualifier).
The quote states multi-account support allows up to 20 VPCs or up to six transit gateways from multiple accounts per Direct Connect gateway.
The quote states each connection can have one or more VIFs configured for public IP space services or private IP space VPC resources.
The quote says any amount of data can be transferred up to the limit of the selected port capacity.
Under the heading on Layer 2 between VPC and your network, the quote says Layer 2 connections are not supported.
The quote states Direct Connect offers an SLA.
The quote states a private VIF cannot be attached to a transit gateway.
The quote states one private VIF can only attach to one Direct Connect gateway or one virtual private gateway.
Answering whether Regional transfer uses the Direct Connect rate, the quote says inter-AZ transfer is billed at the regular Regional rate.
The quote states Direct Connect requires BGP, which covers the narrower VIF-to-VPC scope of the claim.
The quote states the Resiliency Toolkit provides a connection wizard to choose between resiliency models.
The quote states private and transit VIFs must share the gateway's account while VGWs and transit gateways can be in other accounts.
The quote recommends a second connection and says multiple ports at one location are provisioned on redundant equipment.
The quote states SiteLink at two or more locations sends data between them bypassing Regions and works with hosted and dedicated connections.
The quote states SiteLink requires BGP.
The quote states a transit VIF cannot be attached to a virtual private gateway.
The quote gives the two charges, per port-hour pricing per port type, partial hours billed as full, and the port owner paying port hours.
The quote states a VGW-VPC pair cannot be part of more than one Direct Connect gateway.
The quote defines a VIF as public or private, public for public services such as S3, private for your VPC.
Under the heading on extending a VLAN to AWS, the quote answers no and says VLANs only separate traffic between virtual interfaces.
The quote states VPNs use IPsec over the public internet, configure in minutes, and suit immediate need, low to modest bandwidth and tolerance of internet variability.
The What's New quote states Direct Connect supports resilience testing with FIS to test application response when BGP sessions over VIFs are disrupted.
The quote states a hosted connection cannot be requested in the console, a partner creates and configures it, and you must accept it before use.
The quote defines a hosted connection as a physical Ethernet connection a partner provisions for a customer, requested by contacting a partner.
On the hosted connections page, under the hosted port speed notes, the quote says port speeds can only be changed by your partner.
The quote states hosted connections support only one virtual interface.
The quote states port hours are billed once accepted, continue while provisioned, and stop by cancelling through the partner.
The quote states a hosted VIF serves another account, must be accepted by that owner, and works like a standard VIF to public resources or a VPC.
The quote states all connections in a LAG operate in Active/Active mode.
The quote defines a LAG as a logical interface using LACP to aggregate connections at one endpoint, treated as a single managed connection.
The quote states a maximum of two 100 or 400 Gbps connections or four connections below 100 Gbps in a LAG.
The quote describes the minimum operational connections attribute, default 0 for new LAGs, and the whole LAG going non-operational below a set threshold.
The two quotes state no extra charge for a LAG and that dynamic LACP bundles are used while static ones are not supported.
The quotes state MLAG is not supported and a LAG only includes ports on the same Direct Connect devices.
The quote states a LAG does not add resilience, protects against single link failure with minimum links one, but not against device failure or maintenance.
The quotes require dedicated connections at 1/10/100/400 Gbps and state hosted connections cannot use LAGs.
The two quotes require the same bandwidth and termination at the same Direct Connect endpoint.

The quote supports the session going down above 100 routes and traffic stopping until routes are reduced, but the qualifier adjustable=true is not stated by the quote (and conflicts with adjustable=false on direct-connect-faq-bgp-routes-limit-100).
Both quotes list 1, 10, 100 and 400 Gbps as the dedicated connection port speeds.
The quote states multipath per prefix at up to 16 next-hops wide, each a unique AWS endpoint.
Both quotes list the possible hosted connection speeds from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps.
The quote states the LOA-CFA authority expires if the cross connect is not completed within 90 days and can be downloaded again from the console.
The quote states planned maintenance is scheduled 14 days in advance and typically occurs in a four-hour low-traffic window at the location.

The quote supports that a private VIF MTU can be 1500 or 9001, but the value keyed 'default' (1500) presents 1500 as the default, which the quote does not say; rename the key or add evidence for the default.

The quotes support that a transit VIF MTU can be 1500 or 8500, but the value keyed 'default' (1500) presents 1500 as the default, which neither quote says; rename the key or add evidence for the default.

The table row supports a default of 100 per address family per VIF, but the claim says 'per virtual interface' while the exception (public VIFs are not managed by inbound prefix controls; the qualifier's private and transit scope) stands only in the sentence after the table, not in the quote.

The table row supports 10,000 combined IPv4 and IPv6 per DXGW, but the qualifier condition (prefix controls apply to private and transit VIFs) stands only in the sentence after the table, not in the quote.

The table row supports a maximum of 1,000 per address family per VIF, but the claim says 'per virtual interface' while the public-VIF exception and the qualifier's private and transit scope stand only in the sentence after the table, not in the quote.

The table row supports pools of 5,000 (1/10 Gbps), 30,000 (100 Gbps) and 50,000 (400 Gbps) per dedicated connection, but the qualifier condition (private and transit VIFs only; public VIFs not managed) stands only in the text after the table, not in the quote.
The quote states public VIFs are not managed by inbound prefix controls and keep the existing limit of 1,000 inbound prefixes.
